MAP → MOGG · pointers, shapes and calls

The tensor interface gains a body with four pointers and a context. Follow shape construction, value mapping and the registered call.

Fused attention: Q/K/V = float32[32,32], gpu:0; BN=16, BD=8. Blue blocks show concrete states and transformations. IR names and simplified syntax are schematic. TEST labels identify inspected repository expectations, not tests run for this example.

QnA 1 · What changes from MAP to MOGG for this call?

The outer tensor interface is retained, while the routine body receives pointers, shapes and a context handle. For this static example, its body has five arguments: Q pointer, K pointer, V pointer, output pointer, device context. There are no dynamic-dimension arguments. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:928 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:942 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:963 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:996

BEFORE · map.iter.opaque
  outer operands: Q:T0, K:T0, V:T0
  outer result:   O:T0
  body arguments: Q:T0, K:T0, V:T0, output:T0

AFTER · mogg.routine
  outer operands: Q:T0, K:T0, V:T0
  outer result:   O:T0
  body arguments:
    0  %qptr : !mogg.pointer
    1  %kptr : !mogg.pointer
    2  %vptr : !mogg.pointer
    3  %optr : !mogg.pointer
    4  %ctx  : !mogg.context

T0 = float32[32,32] on gpu:0

!mogg.pointer is a compiler type for a future data-pointer argument. It is not an observed address. Likewise %ctx represents the future kernel device context; it is not the compiler's MLIR context or the shared MAXContext. Later MOGG→MGP supplies it from the model's device arguments. ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:825 ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:894

QnA 2 · What is the expanded MAP→MOGG call stack?

SOURCE · the pass rewrites IR1, the compiler-owned clone. gcPipelineImpl copies opts.enableComputeLambdas into the MAP→MOGG pass options; the default is true. Scheduling the pass only installs this recipe. Its runOnOperation() executes when the pass manager runs IR1. The option affects eligible output epilogues; the ordinary attention output has no such epilogue. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:595 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:654 MAPToMOGG.td:28

The physical block-argument order is inputs → output destinations → dimensions → contexts. The custom printer can display its labeled context (...) group before dims (...); that presentation does not reorder the underlying argument list. QnA 3 · Show the actual shape, tensor and value mappings.

These lines replace the old MAP body arguments with representations suitable for the generated MOGG routine. state.mapping records those replacements so the nested kernel call can use them.

QnA3 shows this connection:

OLD tensor argument
        │
        │ compiler records a replacement
        ▼
NEW tensor view
        ├─ pointer parameter
        ├─ shape
        ├─ dtype
        └─ input/output and storage metadata

This constructs compiler objects describing access to tensor storage. It does not copy Q/K/V/O’s elements or execute attention. The mapping is an MLIR IRMapping, stored in the temporary lowering state for the kernel. See MAPToMOGGState.h:43.

Start with the actual attention example: Q/K/V/O are float32[32,32], with BN=16, BD=8, on gpu:0. The following names are schematic.

BEFORE: old MAP body block

Arguments:
  %qi : T0     ← query tensor
  %ki : T0     ← key tensor
  %vi : T0     ← value tensor
  %oi : T0     ← output destination

Operation:
  map.call.opaque @Attention
    inputs(%qi, %ki, %vi)
    outputs(%oi)

T0 = float32[32,32]

The new MOGG body starts with storage parameters:

AFTER: new MOGG body block

Arguments:
  %qptr : !mogg.pointer
  %kptr : !mogg.pointer
  %vptr : !mogg.pointer
  %optr : !mogg.pointer
  %ctx  : !mogg.context

But the kernel call needs tensor representations, not just bare pointer parameters. The pass therefore builds:

%qptr ──┐
[32,32] ├──► %Q_view : !mogg.tensor   [f32, Input,  mut=false]
        ┘

%kptr ──┐
[32,32] ├──► %K_view : !mogg.tensor   [f32, Input,  mut=false]
        ┘

%vptr ──┐
[32,32] ├──► %V_view : !mogg.tensor   [f32, Input,  mut=false]
        ┘

%optr ──┐
[32,32] ├──► %O_view : !mogg.tensor   [f32, Output, mut=true]
        ┘

The source constructs these views with buildTensor, using each new pointer argument and the original tensor type. See MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1002.

The mapping points to the reconstructed views—not directly to the pointers:

Old MAP body argument state.mapping replacement Pointer used by that view
%qi %Q_view %qptr
%ki %K_view %kptr
%vi %V_view %vptr
%oi %O_view %optr

For Q alone, distinguish these four compiler values:

%q       Graph-level tensor input
 │
 └──► %qi       Old MAP body's tensor argument

%qptr    New MOGG body's pointer parameter
 │
 └──► %Q_view   New tensor representation built around that pointer

state.mapping records: %qi → %Q_view

Their relationship follows the query input through lowering. They are different SSA values defined in different places.

When the pass lowers the nested call, it looks up the replacement for each old operand:

Old call input %qi → lookup → %Q_view
Old call input %ki → lookup → %K_view
Old call input %vi → lookup → %V_view
Old destination %oi → lookup → %O_view

New call:
  mogg.call.opaque @Attention
    inputs(%Q_view, %K_view, %V_view)
    outputs(%O_view)
    context(%ctx)

Those lookups are explicit in CallOpaqueOp::lowerToMOGG:645.

Why is the mapping needed? The new routine has a new body block and new values. Its operations must use those new representations rather than referring to arguments belonging to the old body, which will be erased. MLIR’s mapping utility associates original values with replacement values; region scoping governs where those values can be used. IRMapping documentation · MLIR region scoping

The map is keyed by value identity, not by shape. Q, K and V all have the same type, but that does not make them the same input.

The three input/output branches handle different contracts:

Original value New body argument Reconstructed representation
Ordinary tensor input !mogg.pointer !mogg.tensor, io=Input, mut=false
Buffer input !mogg.pointer !mogg.buffer, io=Input, mut=true
Tensor output destination !mogg.pointer !mogg.tensor, io=Output, mut=true
Opaque input Same opaque type Forward the new argument directly

This distinction is implemented by the input loop, output loop and buildTensor. See the input/output branches and buildTensor.

For a buffer input, consider an existing destination buffer:

Old MAP argument:
  %bi : !mo.buffer<[2,3], f32>

New MOGG argument:
  %bptr : !mogg.pointer

Reconstruction:
  %B_view = tensor.create(%bptr, shape=[2,3])
            result type = !mogg.buffer
            io = Input
            mut = true

Mapping:
  %bi → %B_view

Here, “Input” means the buffer is supplied to the kernel. It does not mean the buffer must be read-only. mut=true preserves its mutable-storage representation; it does not itself perform a write.

There is a useful later-stage nuance: if the chosen implementation only reads that buffer, call conformance can reconstruct an immutable tensor view for that argument. The repository’s fused mutable-load test checks this transition from a mutable !mogg.buffer to an immutable !mogg.tensor. See fused-mutable-load-opaque.mlir:8.

For an opaque input, no tensor reconstruction is appropriate:

Old MAP argument:
  %pair_old : !mo.opaque<"SIMDPair", ...>

New MOGG argument:
  %pair_new : the same opaque type

Mapping:
  %pair_old → %pair_new

No shape.create
No tensor.create
No conversion to a tensor-storage pointer

The new argument is still a different SSA value, but it retains the opaque type and reaches the call directly. A repository test checks this alongside a tensor output that does require pointer-and-shape reconstruction. See opaque-values.mlir:30.

“Opaque input” is different from “input to an opaque operation.” Your attention operation is opaque, but Q/K/V have ordinary tensor types, so they take the tensor branch.

buildShape supplies the dimensions needed by each view. For a static shape:

Original tensor shape: [32,32]

mogg.shape.create()
  shape attribute = [32,32]
  dynamic operands = none

For a generic dynamic-shape comparison:

Original tensor shape: [N,32]

state.dimArgs:
  N → %n

mogg.shape.create(%n)
  shape attribute = [dyn,32]
  dynamic operand = %n

The two compiler maps have different jobs:

state.dimArgs:  dimension symbol N → dimension argument %n
state.mapping: old tensor argument %qi → reconstructed tensor %Q_view

If %n later has value 16, the view describes [16,32]. The shape operation combines the dynamic dimension operand with the constant second dimension. See buildShape:79.

Why carry shape and dtype around a pointer? They determine how the storage is interpreted.

For an illustrative row-major float32[2,3] tensor:

Possible future contents:
  [[10,20,30],
   [40,50,60]]

Element [1,2]:
  element offset = 1×3 + 2 = 5
  byte offset    = 5×4     = 20

pointer + 20 bytes → element 60

The shape supplies the row length 3; dtype supplies the element width 4 bytes. buildTensor records that information. Later emission constructs a row-major layout and the corresponding tensor wrapper. The lowering pass does not read the illustrative value 60. See TensorCreateOp::emitMojo:1504.

The fields on TensorCreateOp carry these meanings:

Field What it contributes
pointer Generated parameter referring to storage
shape Generated shape value, including dynamic dimensions
shapeAttr Original shape description, retaining rank and symbolic shape information
dtype Element interpretation, such as f32
device Kind label such as "gpu"; the routine retains the full gpu:0 reference
io Input or output role
mut Whether the reconstructed view is mutable
stable Whether storage is represented through a stable address slot

These fields are declared in MOGGOps.td:1097.

stable has a particular storage meaning; it does not mean the tensor’s values are constant:

Ordinary storage:
  pointer parameter ──► tensor payload

Stable-slot storage:
  pointer parameter ──► address slot ──► current tensor payload

The flag is copied from the source tensor type. When it is set, later emission constructs a StableTensor over that slot. See the stable-type definition.

There are finally two distinct replacement steps:

Inside the kernel:
  old %oi destination → new %O_view
  recorded through state.mapping

At the enclosing graph:
  old iterator result %o_MAP → new routine result %o_MOGG
  users are redirected, then the old iterator is erased

The new routine and its view operations remain in IR1. The temporary mapping helped construct them; it is not a runtime table used during every attention execution. The graph still takes Q/K/V and returns O. See lowering completion:1038.

Source details · original attention IR, input/output value mappings and structural test evidence

The following is source-derived schematic IR, with shortened attribute spelling and package names. The pass initially calls buildShape for each tensor; a later cleanup can share identical shape operations. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:102

%o = mogg.routine(%q:T0,%k:T0,%v:T0) -> T0
  body(%qptr,%kptr,%vptr,%optr : !mogg.pointer,
       %ctx : !mogg.context) {

    %sq = mogg.shape.create() {shape=[32,32]}
    %Q  = mogg.tensor.create(%qptr,%sq)
          {elementType=f32, device="gpu", io=Input, mut=false}

    %sk = mogg.shape.create() {shape=[32,32]}
    %K  = mogg.tensor.create(%kptr,%sk)
          {elementType=f32, device="gpu", io=Input, mut=false}

    %sv = mogg.shape.create() {shape=[32,32]}
    %V  = mogg.tensor.create(%vptr,%sv)
          {elementType=f32, device="gpu", io=Input, mut=false}

    %so = mogg.shape.create() {shape=[32,32]}
    %O  = mogg.tensor.create(%optr,%so)
          {elementType=f32, device="gpu", io=Output, mut=true}

    mogg.call.opaque @PKG.fused_attention.FusedAttention
      inputs(%Q,%K,%V) outputs(%O) context(%ctx)
      parameters={BD=8,BN=16}
  } device=gpu:0
Old MAP body value state.mapping target Meaning
%qi %Q read-only query view over %qptr
%ki %K read-only key view over %kptr
%vi %V read-only value view over %vptr
%oi %O writable output view over %optr

The mapping is populated for inputs and destinations before lowering the nested call. The full gpu:0 ref remains on the routine; the reconstructed tensor operations record the kind label "gpu". ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:916 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1011 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1018

QnA 4 · Why no dimension arguments for [32,32]? What if N were dynamic?

QnA4 explains when the generated MOGG routine needs extra arguments to carry tensor dimensions, in addition to its four pointers and device context.

For your actual attention example, Q/K/V/O all have shape [32,32]. Both axis lengths are known during compilation, so the compiler can put 32,32 directly into each shape construction. MLIR distinguishes dimensions known during compilation from dynamic dimensions. (mlir.llvm.org)

STATIC: Q, K, V, O each [32,32]

routine body:
  %qp   %kp   %vp   %op   %ctx
   Q     K     V     O    context

4 pointers + 0 dimension arguments + 1 context = 5 arguments

Shape construction:
  mogg.shape.create() {shape=[32,32]}
                    ↑
             no dimension operand needed

The source collects only dynamic dimensions and adds body arguments for those collected dimensions. The constant 32 entries therefore add no dimension arguments. See the collector.

QnA4 then gives a generic dynamic-shape comparison: suppose all four tensors have shape [N,32], where N is not known during compilation.

DYNAMIC: Q, K, V, O each [N,32]

routine body:
  %qp   %kp   %vp   %op   %n   %ctx
   Q     K     V     O     N   context

4 pointers + 1 dimension argument + 1 context = 6 arguments

%n carries the dimension value needed to reconstruct those tensor views. There is one %n, shared across all four tensors, because they use the same symbolic N. See dimension argument creation.

mogg.shape.create(%n) {shape=[dyn,32]}
                  │            │
                  └────────────┘
              supplies the dynamic axis length

If %n = 16 → reconstructed shape [16,32]
If %n = 32 → reconstructed shape [32,32]

dyn marks the position of a dynamic dimension; %n supplies its value. The compiler retains the constant second dimension, 32, directly in the shape attribute. See buildShape.

The extra %n belongs to the generated routine’s body. It is not another user tensor input. QnA4 is explaining why your static example has five body arguments, while the illustrated dynamic case has six.

Source details · static dimension attributes, shared symbols and the original argument-count comparison

The collector treats a concrete KGEN::SIMDAttr dimension as static. All eight dimension entries across Q/K/V/O are the constant 32, so none needs a runtime dimension argument. This scalar dimension attribute is separate from the tensors' float32 element type. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:41 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:48

This example: Q,K,V,O each [32,32]
  unique dynamic dimensions = {}
  body argument count = 4 pointers + 0 dims + 1 context = 5

Comparison: Q,K,V,O each [N,32], using the SAME symbolic N
  unique dynamic dimensions = {N}
  body argument count = 4 pointers + 1 dim + 1 context = 6
  additional argument: %n : !mogg.dim<N>
  shape construction: mogg.shape.create(%n) {shape=[dyn,32]}

The dynamic shape attribute uses a common dyn spelling; the operand %n retains the actual dimension value. If N later equals 32, the view describes 1,024 elements, but its dimension path is still different from a compile-time constant [32,32]. Distinct symbolic names are not merged solely because they may happen to have equal runtime values. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:76 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:87 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:963

QnA 5 · Where do BN, BD, dtype, rank and target get their values?

The phases are different. MAP→MOGG preserves the explicit parameter dictionary and prepares typed call operands; it does not turn BN/BD into tensor inputs. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:675 ↗ ParameterInference.cpp:63

Item Value Where it comes from / when consumed
BN 16 Python caller → custom dict → MAP/MOGG call attribute
BD 8 Python caller → custom dict → MAP/MOGG call attribute
dtype float32 tensor element type; inferred by Mojo from the call argument types
rank 2 tensor shape rank; declared before // in execute
target "gpu" later emitter reads the outlined function's device label
ctx future GPU context handle routine context argument → later runtime device argument

Sources: example arguments, infer-only parameter handling, emitter default inference and context wiring. ↗ fused_attention.py:38 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:74 ↗ ParameterInference.cpp:328 ↗ EmitMojoState.cpp:582 ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:831

The eventual implementation call can be understood as this abbreviated Mojo call, with module qualification and setup omitted:

FusedAttention.execute[BN=16, BD=8, target="gpu"](
    output, query, key, value, ctx
)

Notice the implementation's output-first order. mogg.call.opaque keeps separate input/output lists, and the emitter puts outputs first when it writes Mojo. Dtype and rank are inferred; explicitly supplying those infer-only parameters is unnecessary. ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:1892 ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:1918 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:77

QnA 6 · What is ready for the MOGG refinement stage?

IR1
├─ mo.graph @fused_attention
│  └─ mogg.routine : (T0,T0,T0) → T0
│     ├─ body: 4 pointer arguments + 1 context argument
│     ├─ typed Q/K/V/O view construction
│     └─ mogg.call.opaque to P1 declaration, BN=16, BD=8
└─ kernel declarations retained for later conformance and emission

G1 Python members: retained
Runtime output allocation: still to be planned
Next: conform call operands → outline this body → trace/cleanup

These are code-generation operations, not PTX or machine instructions. The next stage gives the body a callable symbol while retaining the routine's tensor boundary for MOGG→MGP. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:370 ↗ OutlineRoutines.cpp:14 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:618

QnA 7 · How do concrete MAP bodies become MOGG calls, views and by-value results while preserving their computation?

SOURCE · eight worked transformations. The before/after IR below is schematic: names and type spellings are shortened, and each pointer names a future buffer reference. Numerical values and byte offsets are illustrative arithmetic, not captured execution. TEST paragraphs describe inspected repository inputs and expectations. A test's RUN command parses that file and invokes passes; production lowering does not call the .mlir file. CHECK matches required output, CHECK-NEXT also requires adjacency, and CHECK-NOT excludes a match within its check interval.

Example 1 · How does the fused-attention call acquire four pointers and a device context without changing Q, K, V or O?

The 15.5 paragraph illustrates the intended attention result. It does not explain how four pointers are introduced. I placed the numerical example before the structural explanation, which made the connection unclear.

The pointer count comes from three tensor inputs plus one tensor output destination:

Tensor role       Generated pointer parameter
───────────       ───────────────────────────
Q input       →   %qp
K input       →   %kp
V input       →   %vp
O destination →   %op

                  FOUR pointer parameters

The lowering code creates one pointer argument for each tensor input, then one for each tensor output. The number comes from those tensor roles—not their values, their [32,32] shape or their two axes. See MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:942.

The actual transformation is schematically:

BEFORE: MAP describes tensors

attention(
    inputs:  Q, K, V,
    output:  O
)


AFTER: MOGG creates a routine body with storage parameters

routine body(%qp, %kp, %vp, %op, %ctx)
              │    │    │    │     │
              Q    K    V    O     device context

These are compiler-level parameters, not actual GPU addresses obtained during this pass. An MLIR block argument represents a value supplied when that block executes. Here, the compiler declares pointer parameters; this step does not allocate the tensor payloads. (mlir.llvm.org) See the argument creation.

A pointer alone does not describe a tensor’s shape or dtype, so the routine reconstructs tensor views around those parameters:

%qp + shape [32,32] + float32 + input/read-only → Q view
%kp + shape [32,32] + float32 + input/read-only → K view
%vp + shape [32,32] + float32 + input/read-only → V view
%op + shape [32,32] + float32 + output/writable → O view

These four views are passed to P1's attention implementation.

The compiler maps the old MAP tensor arguments to these new views. It changes how the tensors are represented and supplied to the implementation; it does not compute their elements. See the tensor reconstruction and mapping.

Why the fifth argument, %ctx? The routine creates a context argument, and the attention implementation’s signature declares ctx: DeviceContext, so the nested call forwards it. The routine retains gpu:0 for later device-context resolution. %ctx is separate from the four tensor pointers. See context argument creation and context forwarding.

The graph’s public interface still has three inputs and one result. %op is the internal output-storage parameter; it does not become a fourth user input.

The 15.5 illustration was intended to show what the unchanged attention calculation would produce for those hypothetical arrays. Changing those arrays would change the result, but the routine would still need the same four pointer parameters.

      │     └─ operations

The four mogg.tensor.create objects retain the shape/dtype and input/output roles; their device label is "gpu", while the routine retains gpu:0. All extents are static, so this body has zero !mogg.dim arguments. The four shape objects are shown before later CSE can share identical constructions. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:79 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:102 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:917 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:962

Temporary compiler mapping: state.mapping
  old %qi → new %Q view over %qp
  old %ki → new %K view over %kp
  old %vi → new %V view over %vp
  old %oi → new %O view over %op

Completion
  replace uses of %o_MAP with %o_MOGG
  erase I_MAP, its old region/body and CALL_MAP
  retain R_MOGG and its newly constructed body in IR1

The mapping targets tensor views, not bare pointers. The outer graph still has three tensor arguments and one tensor result; the five arguments belong to the generated routine's body block. ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1002 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1038

Source detail · native construction, shape/view mapping, context guards and existing structural tests

IterOpaqueOp::lowerToMOGG creates the outer replacement with the old result types, inputs and input chain, then copies memory effects and dispatch. Thus a result-producing kernel and a side-effect-only kernel keep their respective graph contracts. The following is an unchanged implementation excerpt. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:928

auto kernel = MOGG::RoutineOp::create(builder, loc, resultTypes, inputs,
                                      inputChain, fusionInfo);
kernel.setDeviceRef(state.device);

Inside that new routine, four tensor-like positions produce four !mogg.pointer arguments. buildTensor then records shape, dtype, input/output role and mutability around each pointer. There is no dynamic symbol to add between those pointers and %ctx. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:942 buildTensor:102

The new body owns its shape and view operations; state.mapping rewires the old %qi/%ki/%vi/%oi body values to %Q/%K/%V/%O. After the nested call has been lowered, the pass redirects users of the old iterator results and erases the old iterator, including its region. For an illustrative row-major f32 layout, Q's element [2,3] remains at byte offset (2*32+3)*4 = 268 from Q's eventual data pointer. The type describes 4096 payload bytes per tensor; this pass does not allocate those bytes. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1002 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1038

The context guard is signature-driven. This excerpt forwards contexts for a declarative launch or an execute signature ending in a context argument. CallOpaqueOp::lowerToMOGG:668

if (const auto &fn = adaptor.executeFunction;
    adaptor.isDeclarative() ||
    (fn && !fn->inputArguments.empty() &&
     (fn->inputArguments.back().isContextType() ||
      fn->inputArguments.back().isVariadicContextType())))
  contexts = state.contextArgs;
Signature branch Routine body Implementation call
attention declares DeviceContext four pointers + one context %ctx is forwarded
host-only comparison declares no context its body still has the ordinary trailing context argument call omits context(...)
distributed comparison declares DeviceContextArray one context per unique device, at least one contexts remain separate here; the next conformance pass packs them

Example 2 · How does a shared dynamic dimension become one body argument, including dimensions hidden inside a view?

Use the test's shape [batch,4] for both input and output. If batch=3, each tensor describes 12 f32 elements; if batch=5, it describes 20. These are alternative runtime extents of the same compiled shape contract. The example's fixture leaves tensor computation unspecified; the transformation preserves its input, output and selected call. dyn-opaque.mlir:22

BEFORE · schematic MAP
%y = map.iter.opaque inputs(%xi=%x:[batch,4])       # Bind one dynamic tensor.
                    outputs(%yo:[batch,4]) {       # Reuse the same symbolic batch.
  map.call.opaque @OnePlain inputs(%xi) outputs(%yo) # Keep the declared kernel call.
}

COLLECTION
[batch,4] input  → insert batch                   # First occurrence creates one map entry.
[batch,4] output → reuse batch                    # Attribute identity deduplicates it.
4               → skip                          # Concrete dimension needs no SSA argument.

The collector inserts each non-static dimension into a MapVector. Later, buildShape stores a common dyn placeholder in the shape attribute but connects the actual dimension through an SSA operand. These are implementation excerpts, showing the collection and reconstruction at their respective call sites. dynamicDimWalker:48 buildShape:87

for (Attribute dim : shape.getValues())
  if (isDynamicDim(dim))
    state.dimArgs.insert({dim, BlockArgument()});
if (isDynamicDim(dim)) {
  dims.push_back(state.dimArgs.lookup(dim));
  canonicalDims.push_back(canonicalDyn);
} else {
  canonicalDims.push_back(dim);
}
AFTER · schematic MOGG
%y = mogg.routine(%x:[batch,4]) -> [batch,4] {      # Retain tensor-level types.
  body(%xp:pointer,%yp:pointer,%b:dim<batch>,%ctx)  # Two pointers + one dim + context.
  %sx = shape.create(%b) {shape=[dyn,4]}           # Use batch for the input extent.
  %X = tensor.create(%xp,%sx,f32,Input,false)      # Same future input storage.
  %sy = shape.create(%b) {shape=[dyn,4]}           # Same dimension SSA operand.
  %Y = tensor.create(%yp,%sy,f32,Output,true)      # Separate output destination.
  call.opaque @OnePlain inputs(%X) outputs(%Y) context(%ctx) # Preserve the call.
}

CSE may later share %sx and %sy because both their attributes and operands match. For input [M,4] and output [N,4], the two shape attributes can both print [dyn,4], but %m and %n are distinct operands. Runtime coincidence M=N=3 is not enough for this pass to merge them. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:76

TEST · shared symbol. dyn-opaque.mlir:1 starts with MO and runs package import → MO→MAP → MAP→MOGG. Its checks name one !mogg.dim<batch> and require that same captured SSA name in both mogg.shape.create operations. They check dimension wiring, not a measured choice of batch size. dyn-opaque.mlir:13

A dimension can also occur only in a nested view. The collector walks nested operation attributes and operand/result types, so it includes the axis reduced away from a kernel's output. collectDynamicDims:65 IterOpaqueOp::lowerToMOGG:937

Comparison before lowering
%x : [D0,D1,D2,D3]                               # Four input dimensions.

Illustrative permutation [2,0,3,1]
input [2,3,4,5] → view [4,2,5,3] → output [4,2,5,1] # Reduced extent remains 3.

Example 3 · How does a transposed MAP view become a MOGG view and a loop that writes the same matrix?

A stride view describes a different way to index existing tensor storage. MAP→MOGG converts that description into a MOGG tensor-view operation, then rewrites the consuming loop to use it.

For transpose, the important transformation is:

MAP:
  map.index.transpose.stride

              ↓ lowering

MOGG:
  mogg.tensor.create.transpose

The MOGG operation represents a zero-copy transpose view. A later loop may still read that view and write a separate output tensor. Those are two different actions. See the operation definition.

Start with this illustrative matrix:

X: shape [2,3]

                 column
               0   1   2
             ┌───┬───┬───┐
       row 0 │ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │
             ├───┼───┼───┤
       row 1 │ 4 │ 5 │ 6 │
             └───┴───┴───┘

Assume dense row-major float32 storage:

Physical element order:
  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Element offsets:
   0  1  2  3  4  5

Byte offsets:
   0  4  8 12 16 20

Its element strides are [3,1]:

Advance one row    → advance 3 elements
Advance one column → advance 1 element

X[row,column] offset = row×3 + column×1

A stride is the distance between adjacent elements along an axis. Strided representations let a view describe different indexing over existing storage. MLIR · strided storage and transpose.

The permutation [1,0] means:

Output axis 0 comes from input axis 1
Output axis 1 comes from input axis 0

                    INPUT             TRANSPOSE VIEW
Shape:              [2,3]       →     [3,2]
Element strides:    [3,1]       →     [1,3]

Therefore the view looks like:

TV: shape [3,2]

               column
                0   1
              ┌───┬───┐
        row 0 │ 1 │ 4 │
              ├───┼───┤
        row 1 │ 2 │ 5 │
              ├───┼───┤
        row 2 │ 3 │ 6 │
              └───┴───┘

TV[i,j] refers to X[j,i]

The backing primitive implements precisely this: it permutes the input dimensions and strides, then returns a view using the same input pointer. It does not rearrange the six elements. See primitives.mojo:2665.

X view:
  pointer = PX
  shape   = [2,3]
  strides = [3,1]

TV view:
  pointer = PX          ← same storage
  shape   = [3,2]
  strides = [1,3]        ← different indexing

What does TransposeStrideOp::lowerToMOGG actually do?

It reads the old view’s contract, looks up the already-lowered operands, creates the new view operation, and records its result in state.mapping:

Native expression What it supplies
getSpec().getSignature() Input/output shape relationship
signature.getOut() Transposed view’s shape, here [3,2]
getSpec().getPerm() Known permutation entries, here [1,0]
Input element type f32, unchanged
state.mapping.lookup(getInput()) Reconstructed MOGG input view
state.mapping.lookup(getPermutations()) Reconstructed permutation tensor
state.mapping.map(getResult(), ...) Replacement for the old MAP view result

See MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:777.

Schematically:

OLD MAP values:
  %xi       input tensor argument
  %permOld  permutation tensor argument
  %tv       result of transpose.stride

Existing mappings:
  %xi      → %X_view
  %permOld → %PERM_view

New operation:
  %TV = mogg.tensor.create.transpose(%X_view,%PERM_view)
          outShape=[3,2]
          staticPermutations=[1,0]
          elementType=f32

New mapping:
  %tv → %TV

Notice the dependency: the base input view must exist before the transpose view can be constructed.

Input pointer parameter
        │
        ▼
Base tensor view %X_view
        │
        ▼
Transpose view %TV
        │
        ▼
Consumer loads through %TV

This is why the earlier state.mapping work matters. The transpose lowering needs the new input representation, not an argument belonging to the old MAP body.

What happens to the loop?

In this example, MAP view motion has already moved the view construction outside the elementwise body. The loop still iterates over the output domain [3,2]:

BEFORE · schematic MAP

%tv = map.index.transpose.stride(%xi,%permOld)

elementwise body: shape=[3,2], captures(output,%tv)
  for logical index %i:
    %v = map.load %tv[%i]
    map.store output[%i] = %v

MAP→MOGG produces the corresponding view and foreach operation:

AFTER · schematic MOGG

%TV = mogg.tensor.create.transpose(%X_view,%PERM_view)

mogg.call.foreach:
  loop shape = [3,2]
  captures   = [%O_view,%TV]

  body arguments:
    %oArg     ← captured output view
    %tvArg    ← captured transpose view
    %i        ← current two-coordinate index

  %v = mogg.tensor.load %tvArg[%i]
  mogg.tensor.store %oArg[%i] = %v

The foreach lowering maps the old capture arguments and index argument to new body arguments before lowering the load and store. See MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:807.

The loop index does not need to be explicitly swapped in this final load. The transpose view already incorporates that mapping:

Loop index %i = [0,1]
        │
        ▼
load TV[0,1]
        │ view uses strides [1,3]
        ▼
input element offset = 0×1 + 1×3 = 3
        │
        ▼
read X[1,0] = 4
        │
        ▼
store O[0,1] = 4

For the entire matrix:

Loop index Original input read Value Input byte offset Output byte offset
[0,0] X[0,0] 1 0 0
[0,1] X[1,0] 4 12 4
[1,0] X[0,1] 2 4 8
[1,1] X[1,1] 5 16 12
[2,0] X[0,2] 3 8 16
[2,1] X[1,2] 6 20 20

The offsets assume separate dense row-major input and output buffers. These values illustrate the indexing; the repository test checks the generated view, loop shape, load and store operations rather than executing these particular arrays. See transpose-stride.mlir:18.

This exposes the difference between a view and a materialized result:

Transpose view:
  PX ──► original storage [1,2,3,4,5,6]
         interpreted with shape [3,2], strides [1,3]

Standalone transpose output, when the generated loop executes:
  PO ──► output storage [1,4,2,5,3,6]
         dense shape [3,2], strides [2,1]

The view itself shares storage. The standalone transpose’s loop writes the final output. If an eligible consumer uses the view directly, a separate intermediate transpose buffer may be unnecessary.

The compiler conversion constructs the operations describing this work; it does not perform those runtime loads and stores. The test’s pipeline shows view motion followed by MAP→MOGG lowering. See transpose-stride.mlir:1.

Why are there both static permutation attributes and a permutation tensor operand?

The operation can represent permutation entries known during compilation and entries known only during execution:

Fully static:
  staticPermutations = [1,0]
  use those entries directly

Runtime permutation:
  unknown entries in staticPermutations
  obtain those entries from the permutation tensor

For a fully static permutation, the emitted primitive does not read the permutation tensor at runtime. The operand remains part of the operation’s interface. See MOGGOps.cpp:1740.

The same rule extends beyond swapping two axes:

3D input:
  shape   = [2,3,4]
  strides = [12,4,1]

Permutation [2,0,1]:
  output axis 0 ← input axis 2
  output axis 1 ← input axis 0
  output axis 2 ← input axis 1

Transpose view:
  shape   = [4,2,3]
  strides = [1,12,4]

TV[a,b,c] = X[b,c,a]

That nontrivial permutation is also covered by transpose-stride.mlir:48.

The other stride-view branches use the same general idea, but different index mappings:

View Example How an output index addresses the input
Slice X[1:8:2] view[i] = X[1+2i]
Broadcast [1,3] → [2,3] view[i,j] = X[0,j]
Reshape [2,3] → [3,2] Preserve row-major element order
Transpose [2,3] → [3,2] view[i,j] = X[j,i]

These lower to their respective mogg.tensor.create.* view operations. See MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:692.

For the same six input values, reshape and transpose therefore produce different logical matrices:

Reshape [3,2]:          Transpose [3,2]:

  [[1,2],                [[1,4],
   [3,4],                 [2,5],
   [5,6]]                 [3,6]]

In your attention example, the internal QKᵀ calculation remains inside P1’s authored implementation. This worked example concerns a graph-visible transpose operation, not a separate transpose extracted from the attention kernel. See the attention implementation.

Native rewrite and repository test details

SOURCE · native rewrite. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:777

auto createTranspose = MOGG::TensorCreateTransposeOp::create(
    state.builder, getLoc(), MOGG::TensorType::get(ctx), signature.getOut(),
    getSpec().getPerm(), TypeAttr::get(elementType),
    state.builder.getBoolAttr(viewsMutableStorage(getInput())),
    state.mapping.lookup(getInput()),
    state.mapping.lookup(getPermutations()));
state.mapping.map(getResult(), createTranspose.getResult());

TEST · pass entry and checks. transpose-stride.mlir:36 supplies an MO transpose and a constant permutation. Its RUN pipeline performs import → MO→MAP → structured-body outlining → loop-invariant view motion → iterator canonicalization → MAP→MOGG. CHECK-NEXT verifies pointer reconstruction, the transpose view, the [3,2] foreach domain and the exact load/store sequence. The earlier canonicalizer removes dead original captures after view motion; MAP→MOGG lowers the surviving capture list. The second case checks permutation [2,0,1] from [2,3,4] to [4,2,3]. transpose-stride.mlir:18 transpose-stride.mlir:48

Example 4 · How can a broadcast loop cover 512 output elements while reading only a 64-element input view?

The test broadcasts X:[1,64] to O:[8,64]. Choose illustrative values X[0,c]=c. Every output row must contain 0…63; for example, O[7,5]=5. The broadcast view and the loop domain both describe [8,64], while the original input still describes only 64 elements. broadcast-stride.mlir:30

BEFORE · schematic MAP after view motion
%bv = map.index.broadcast.stride(%X) out=[8,64]   # Broadcast the size-one first axis.
map.iter.elementwise.body shape=[8,64] captures(%O,%bv) { # Use the output domain.
  %v = map.load %bv[%row,%col]                    # Read X[0,col] for each row.
  map.store %O[%row,%col] = %v                    # Materialize the requested output.
}

The native rewrite records signature.getOut() on the view and keeps the input reference. It does not attach a second copy of the input shape to that view. BroadcastStrideOp::lowerToMOGG:721

auto createBroadcast = MOGG::TensorCreateBroadcastOp::create(
    state.builder, getLoc(), MOGG::TensorType::get(ctx), signature.getOut(),
    TypeAttr::get(elementType),
    state.builder.getBoolAttr(viewsMutableStorage(getInput())),
    state.mapping.lookup(getInput()));
state.mapping.map(getResult(), createBroadcast.getResult());

IterElementwiseBodyOp explicitly obtains the iteration shape from the MAP loop's $shape, because a broadcast input can have smaller extents. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:793

AFTER · schematic MOGG
%BV = mogg.tensor.create.broadcast(%X) outShape=[8,64] # Wrap the existing input view.
%loop = mogg.shape.create([8,64])                 # Preserve 8×64 iteration extents.
mogg.call.foreach shape(%loop) captures(%O,%BV) { # Forward two view references.
  %v = mogg.tensor.load %broadcastArg[%i]         # Repeated rows use the same input row.
  mogg.tensor.store %outputArg[%i] = %v           # Store 512 logical output elements.
}

For illustrative row-major f32 addressing, all eight output positions [r,5] read input byte offset 5*4=20. Output [7,5] is stored at (7*64+5)*4=1812 from the output base. No 512-element intermediate input buffer is created by tensor.create.broadcast; the enclosing routine still exposes its separate 512-element output contract.

TEST · two broadcast forms. broadcast-stride.mlir:1 enters at MO and uses the same import, MO→MAP, outlining, view-motion, iterator-cleanup and MAP→MOGG sequence as the transpose test. @broadcastSameRank requires a [1,64] input view, [8,64] output view, broadcast view, and a foreach capturing only output plus broadcast. @broadcastRankExpanding starts with [64] and checks the same output view shape; the input's own rank remains available through its producer. broadcast-stride.mlir:14 broadcast-stride.mlir:42

Example 5 · How are slice offsets preserved, and why does a negative start on a dynamic axis lose its static hint?

Use X:[10,64], start=[1,32], stop=[4,64], step=[1,1]; the output shape is [3,32]. With illustrative values X[r,c]=100*r+c, output [2,5] is X[3,37]=337. slice-stride.mlir:37

BEFORE · schematic MAP after view motion
%sv = map.index.slice.stride(%X,%start,%stop,%step) # Preserve runtime bounds as operands.
      in=[10,64], out=[3,32], starts=[1,32], steps=[1,1] # Retain known static hints.
map.iter.elementwise.body shape=[3,32] captures(%O,%sv) { # Loop over slice coordinates.
  %v = map.load %sv[%i]                          # Read X[i0+1,i1+32].
  map.store %O[%i] = %v                         # Write the same element to O.
}

The native implementation first copies the static-start hints. It replaces a hint only when that start is negative and its corresponding input extent is dynamic. SliceStrideOp::lowerToMOGG:699

SmallVector<int64_t> inDims = signature.getIn().getIntDims();
SmallVector<int64_t> staticStart =
    llvm::to_vector(getSpec().getStarts().asArrayRef());
for (size_t i = 0; i < staticStart.size(); ++i)
  if (staticStart[i] < 0 && ShapedType::isDynamic(inDims[i]))
    staticStart[i] = ShapedType::kDynamic;

It then creates mogg.tensor.create.slice with the output shape, static hints, mapped input and all three bounds tensors. Thus removing a static hint does not remove the runtime start value. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:709

AFTER · static example, schematic MOGG
%SV = mogg.tensor.create.slice(%X,%START,%STOP,%STEP) # Keep the bounds references.
      outShape=[3,32], staticStart=[1,32], staticStep=[1,1] # Both starts stay static.
%loop = mogg.shape.create([3,32])                 # Use the slice output extents.
mogg.call.foreach shape(%loop) captures(%O,%SV) { # Use the hoisted slice view.
  %v = mogg.tensor.load %sliceArg[%i]             # Same X[i0+1,i1+32] access.
  mogg.tensor.store %outArg[%i] = %v              # Preserve the output coordinate.
}

Illustrative f32 addressing for %i=[2,5] is source offset (3*64+37)*4=916 bytes and output offset (2*32+5)*4=276 bytes. The output remains 337 at that logical position.

Input-axis extent and start Static hint after this guard Runtime interpretation
known 10, normalized start 1 1 offset is fixed
symbolic N, start -8 dynamic sentinel needs the actual N and the runtime start operand
symbolic N, start 2 2 already an absolute start; no N needed 
Dynamic negative-start comparison, step=1 and runtime stop=N
X:[N,64], start=[-8,0]                            # Request the last eight rows.
  → slice view staticStart=[dynamic,0]            # Defer the extent-dependent offset.
N=20 → resolved first row 12 → output [8,64]      # 20-8 = 12.
N=32 → resolved first row 24 → output [8,64]      # 32-8 = 24.

Its static checks require the [3,32] view and load/store loop; its runtime-bounds case checks that the view still receives four operands. The negative-start case explicitly expects the printed sentinel -9223372036854775808, while the positive-start dynamic case expects 2. These expectations directly exercise the condition above. slice-stride.mlir:15 slice-stride.mlir:50 slice-stride.mlir:72 slice-stride.mlir:91

Example 6 · When can an output epilogue yield a value for the kernel to store, and when must it retain its own store?

Use the test's visible graph O = matmul(A,B) + Z, with all tensors f32[8,8] on gpu:0. For illustrative values A=I, B=2I, Z=all_ones, the required O has diagonal 3 and off-diagonal 1. The earlier MAP fusion pass has placed the add in the matmul's output epilogue; MAP→MOGG chooses how to represent that already-fused body. compute-fused-opaque.mlir:23

BEFORE · schematic MAP epilogue after fusion and accumulating-buffer setup
%epi = map.iter.epilogue(%value:f32,%i) captures(%O,%Z) { # Kernel supplies one result value.
  %z = map.load %Z[%i]                          # Read the residual at that index.
  %sum = map.call.elementwise @Add(%value,%z)    # Compute matmul value + residual.
  map.store %O[%i] = %sum                       # Store once at the unchanged index.
}
map.call.opaque @Matmul inputs(%A,%B) outputs(%epi) # Output declaration permits compute fusion.

classifyEpilogueLambdaKind uses the consuming call's actual declaration. It requires a single opaque-call output use and an eligible compute-output slot. Multiple stores or a transformed store index force the store form; unsupported tile-output slots report an error. The final checks require the option to be enabled and equal incoming/outgoing element types. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:345 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:380

if (!state.enableComputeLambdas)
  return Kind::OutputLegacyForCompute;
Type inType = epilogueOp.getBody().getArgument(0).getType();
Type outType = cast<MO::TensorType>(result.getType()).getElementType();
if (inType != outType)
  return Kind::OutputLegacyForCompute;

return Kind::Compute;

In the matched case, IterEpilogueOp::lowerToMOGG lowers the arithmetic but skips the store to the designated output capture. It remembers that store's mapped value and creates mogg.yield with it. The output capture and output pointer remain so the emitter can bind the functor to the destination. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:521 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:553

AFTER · enabled, eligible compute epilogue
%epi = mogg.tensor.create.epilogue(%value:simd<f32>,%i) # Preserve value and index inputs.
       captures(%O,%Z), computeOutputArg=true {       # Retain destination metadata.
  %z = mogg.tensor.load %Z[%i]                      # Same residual read.
  %sum = mogg.call.elementwise @Add(%value,%z)       # Same addition.
  mogg.yield %sum                                   # Kernel performs the final store.
}
call.opaque @Matmul inputs(%A,%B) outputs(%epi)       # Same matmul implementation.

AFTER · enable-compute-lambdas=false
%epi = mogg.tensor.create.epilogue(%value:simd<f32>,%i) # Same output contract.
       captures(%O,%Z), computeOutputArg=true {       # Slot still declares compute capability.
  %z = mogg.tensor.load %Z[%i]                      # Same residual read.
  %sum = mogg.call.elementwise @Add(%value,%z)       # Same addition.
  mogg.tensor.store %O[%i] = %sum                   # Functor owns the store instead.
}

At an illustrative diagonal element both routes calculate 2+1=3; elsewhere both calculate 0+1=1. computeOutputArg=true records the kernel argument's contract even when the body uses the store fallback. It does not by itself prove that the body ends in a yield. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:508

Guard Matched case Skipped or rejected case
eligible consumer contract compute-output slot ordinary store-output slot keeps store form
output stores one destination multiple destinations keep stores
index mapping store at incoming index reshape/index transform keeps store ownership
dtype incoming f32 → outgoing f32 incoming f32 → outgoing si32 keeps cast and store
option enabled disabled uses store fallback
tile fused-output contract SIMD case supported here tile case reports unsupported MAP epilogue fusion

Its @mixed_dtype case checks the retained store after an f32-to-si32 cast. Example 7 · How does a shape-function invocation become a host routine that returns dimensions by value?

The repository test supplies a shape-only gather invocation with input shape [1,2,3], indices shape [4,5], axis=-2, and four declared output dimensions. For the ordinary gather shape rule, axis -2 in rank 3 means axis 1; replacing that input axis with the indices shape gives [1,4,5,3]. The test then broadcasts scalar integer 1 into that shape, describing 60 ones. It does not perform a data gather; its indices tensor's f32 element type is used only as a source of shape metadata in this fixture. shape-func-kgen-params.mlir:11 gather_shape_fn:2096 gather_shape:1579

BEFORE · schematic MO operation remaining among the MAP work
mo.invoke_shape_func "mo.gather"(%input:[1,2,3],%indices:[4,5]) # Ask for four extents.
  outputParams=[D4,D5,D6,D7], kgenParams={axis=-2}              # Preserve axis as a parameter.
%one = constant(1) : scalar<si32>                            # Test's data value is one.
%out = broadcast(%one) : [D4,D5,D6,D7]                       # Use the returned shape.

The MAP→MOGG pass handles these invocations in a second walk after its opaque-iterator worklist. lowerInvokeShapeFuncToMOGG looks up the registered shape function, creates a routine with result type !mogg.shape_func_result<4> and copies the output parameter declarations. Missing registration produces a diagnostic; the pass cannot invent the shape computation. MAPToMOGG.cpp:73 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:134

The call's parameter dictionary is built from the output rank and normalized original kgenParams. Forwarding only rank would lose the axis argument required by the implementation. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:179

SmallVector<NamedAttribute> shapeParams{
    builder.getNamedAttr(MOGG::kMoggOutputRankParameterName,
                         builder.getIndexAttr(static_cast<int64_t>(rank)))};
if (DictionaryAttr kgenParams = shapeFuncOp.getKgenParamsAttr())
  for (NamedAttribute param : kgenParams)
    shapeParams.push_back(builder.getNamedAttr(
        param.getName(), normalizeKernelParameter(param.getValue())));
AFTER · schematic shape routine
%shapeResult = mogg.routine(%input,%indices) -> shape_func_result<4> # Return a small shape value.
  outputParams=[D4,D5,D6,D7] {                                  # Retain the dimension bindings.
  body(%inputPtr:pointer,%indicesPtr:pointer,%ctx:context)       # No output data pointer.
  %si = shape.create([1,2,3])                                  # Input extents are static here.
  %I = tensor.create(%inputPtr,%si,f32,Input,false)               # Rebuild the input view.
  %sj = shape.create([4,5])                                    # Indices' own two extents.
  %J = tensor.create(%indicesPtr,%sj,f32,Input,false)             # Rebuild its view.
  %s = mogg.call.shape @gather_shape_fn(%I,%J)                  # Call the registered shape helper.
       params={axis=-2,output_rank=4}, throws                  # Preserve declared parameters/raising behavior.
  mogg.output %s                                              # Return dimensions by value.
}
%out = broadcast(constant(1)) : [D4,D5,D6,D7]                   # Same dependent tensor computation.

The routine body receives a context for the common routine boundary; CallShapeOp receives only its declared data operands. Input pointers and any input dynamic dimensions are arguments, while the four new output dimension declarations remain attached to the routine. The later runtime lowering materializes those shape values for dependent work. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:145 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:158 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:187

TEST · parameter preservation. shape-func-kgen-params.mlir:1 enters at MO with an already-written mo.invoke_shape_func, imports builtin declarations, runs MO→MAP and MAP→MOGG, then checks printed IR. CHECK finds mogg.call.shape …gather_shape_fn; CHECK-SAME requires [axis = -2 : index, output_rank = 4 : index] on that call. The test proves that those parameters survive conversion; [1,4,5,3] and 60 ones above are illustrative shape arithmetic, not a captured result. shape-func-kgen-params.mlir:8

Static attention declares [32,32] directly and has no pending output-dimension declarations requiring this path. ↗ fused_attention.py:57

Example 8 · Why does an opaque value cross the routine boundary differently from an ordinary tensor result?

Use the test's SIMDPair<S0=4,S1=8> value. Its registered producer constructs two integer vectors, [0,1,2,3] and [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11]. Its consumer writes those two vectors into a 12-element output tensor. These values follow from the inspected kernel body; no kernel was executed for this page. testing_kernels.mojo:2996 testing_kernels.mojo:3009

BEFORE · schematic MAP producer
%pair = map.iter.opaque inputs() -> Pair {        # Return a non-tensor aggregate.
  %p = map.call.opaque @MakeSimdPair               # Registration returns the aggregate itself.
       params={P0=4,P1=8} -> Pair                 # Sizes remain type/call parameters.
  map.yield %p                                   # Yield the by-value result.
}

AFTER · schematic MOGG producer
%pair = mogg.routine() -> Pair {                  # Same outer opaque result type.
  body(%ctx:context)                             # No input or output data pointer.
  %p = mogg.call.opaque @MakeSimdPair              # No context on this host-only execute call.
       params={P0=4,P1=8} -> Pair                 # Preserve both vector widths.
  mogg.output %p                                 # Forward the actual opaque SSA result.
}

The ordinary-output loop skips MO::OpaqueType results, so it creates no destination pointer for %pair. The nested call retains an actual result type, maps its result into state.mapping, and the enclosing conversion writes mogg.output for the non-destination value. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:954 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:653 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1028

if (hasOutputChain && i + 1 == e)
  break;
if (isa<MO::OpaqueType>(resultTypes[i]))
  continue;
outputArgs[i] = addBodyArg(resultTypes[i]);

For an opaque input, the conversion adds a block argument with the original opaque type and maps it directly. The consumer's ordinary tensor output still gets a pointer and writable view. MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:945 MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:1005

BEFORE · schematic MAP consumer
%out = map.iter.opaque inputs(%p=%pair:Pair) outputs(%o:si32[12]) { # Mixed value/tensor boundary.
  map.call.opaque @ParameterizedOpaqueType inputs(%p) outputs(%o)  # Store both vector fields.
}

AFTER · schematic MOGG consumer
%out = mogg.routine(%pair:Pair) -> si32[12] {      # Keep the graph's tensor result.
  body(%p:Pair,%op:pointer,%ctx:context)          # Opaque argument stays typed as Pair.
  %shape = shape.create([12])                    # Only the tensor output needs a shape.
  %O = tensor.create(%op,%shape,si32,Output,true) # Construct its destination view.
  mogg.call.opaque @ParameterizedOpaqueType      # Preserve the selected consumer.
    inputs(%p:Pair) outputs(%O) params={P0=4}     # Same opaque data and output location.
}

Future consumer writes, derived from the registered body
O[0:4] = [0,1,2,3]                               # First vector occupies four elements.
O[4:12] = [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11]                   # Second vector occupies eight elements.

TEST · producer and consumer contracts. opaque-values.mlir:1 starts at MO, imports the test package, rewrites public opaque names to their registered types, then runs MO→MAP and MAP→MOGG. @opaque_result checks that no outputs ( destination group exists and that the call result is forwarded by mogg.output. @opaque_input checks the typed opaque block argument beside the tensor output pointer and its shape/view reconstruction. opaque-values.mlir:19 opaque-values.mlir:33

“Opaque” in map.call.opaque identifies a call whose implementation is not expressed as a graph-visible elementwise body. It does not imply that its tensor arguments have !mo.opaque types. The actual attention call uses four ordinary tensor views and therefore retains the pointer-based path in Example 1. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82 ↗ MAPOpsLowerableToMOGG.cpp:643

QnA 8 · What does “create host routine returning !mogg.shape_func_result<rank>” mean? Explain the return type, compiler objects, gather, dynamic dimensions and data-dependent shapes with examples and diagrams.

This line means: the compiler creates a host CPU routine whose return value contains the output tensor’s dimension sizes. For example, !mogg.shape_func_result<4> represents a returned shape containing four dimension sizes. MAP→MOGG builds the routine here; the shape calculation runs when that routine executes. Source: lowering implementation

Let’s connect the type, the generated compiler objects, and some concrete examples.

1. What does !mogg.shape_func_result<rank> contain?

A tensor’s rank is its number of axes. Its shape gives the size of each axis. Rank can be known while the individual sizes are still unknown. MLIR shape inference

For example:

Output tensor shape: [1, 4, 5, 3]
                      │  │  │  │
Axis:                 0  1  2  3

Rank: 4
Number of tensor elements: 1 × 4 × 5 × 3 = 60

Shape-function return value:
    [1, 4, 5, 3]
     └────────┘
     FOUR dimension sizes

Return type:
    !mogg.shape_func_result<4>

The result type records how many dimension sizes are returned. The returned value supplies those sizes. The repository defines this type to lower to a Mojo IndexList of the given rank. Source: type definition

Returned shape value Result type Tensor described by that shape
[32,32] !mogg.shape_func_result<2> Two axes; 1,024 elements
[1,4,5,3] !mogg.shape_func_result<4> Four axes; 60 elements
[N,64], with runtime N=10 !mogg.shape_func_result<2> Two axes; runtime shape [10,64]

These are illustrative values. The shape result contains the dimensions; the tensor’s element values are produced by subsequent tensor computation.

2. Where does the compiler get rank?

The exact code is:

const uint64_t rank = shapeFuncOp.getOutputParamDecls().size();
Type shapeResultType = MOGG::ShapeFuncResultType::get(ctx, rank);

It counts the invocation’s output dimension declarations. Source: lines 145–146

For example:

Shape invocation
└─ outputParamDecls = [D4, D5, D6, D7]
                       │   │   │   │
                       Four declarations
                                │
                                ▼
                             rank = 4
                                │
                                ▼
                  !mogg.shape_func_result<4>

D4, D5, etc. name dimension values that this invocation will define. They become associated with the returned dimension sizes later.

The fallback-shape machinery creates a positional declaration for every output axis, including axes whose sizes are already static. Consequently, this count represents the full returned shape, rather than only its unknown dimensions. Source: positional dimension mapping

3. Example: gather produces the shape [1,4,5,3].

The repository’s test supplies:

Input tensor:   shape [1,2,3]
Indices tensor: shape [4,5]
Gather axis:    -2

For a rank-three input, axis -2 means axis 1. Gather’s shape rule replaces that input axis with the indices tensor’s axes. The registered gather shape helper performs this calculation. Sources: test, shape calculation

Input axes:
    [ 1,        2,        3 ]
      │         │         │
      keep      replace   keep
                  │
                  ▼
Indices axes:   [ 4, 5 ]

Output axes:
    [ 1,        4, 5,     3 ]

Output rank:
    input rank + indices rank − 1
             3 + 2 − 1 = 4

The illustrative returned value is therefore:

shapeResult = [1,4,5,3]
shapeResult type = !mogg.shape_func_result<4>

The helper’s implementation:

  • Normalizes the negative axis.
  • Copies input dimensions before that axis.
  • Inserts all indices dimensions.
  • Copies the remaining input dimensions.

It calculates the shape from the input layouts. This gather shape helper does not inspect the indices’ individual element values. Source: helper body

4. What compiler objects get created?

The following is schematic IR, showing the object relationships rather than exact printable syntax.

Before lowering, the shape invocation remains an MO operation:

mo.invoke_shape_func["mo.gather"](%input, %indices)
├─ outputParamDecls = [D4,D5,D6,D7]
└─ kgenParams = {axis=-2}

MAP→MOGG replaces that invocation with a routine containing a shape-function call:

%shapeResult : !mogg.shape_func_result<4>
└─ defining operation: mogg.routine
   ├─ execution: host CPU
   ├─ inputs: [%input, %indices]
   ├─ outputParamDecls: [D4,D5,D6,D7]
   └─ body
      ├─ arguments
      │  ├─ %inputPtr   : !mogg.pointer
      │  ├─ %indicesPtr : !mogg.pointer
      │  └─ %ctx        : !mogg.context
      │
      ├─ reconstruct input tensor view
      │  └─ pointer=%inputPtr, shape=[1,2,3]
      │
      ├─ reconstruct indices tensor view
      │  └─ pointer=%indicesPtr, shape=[4,5]
      │
      ├─ %s = mogg.call.shape @gather_shape_fn(...)
      │  ├─ parameters: {axis=-2, output_rank=4}
      │  └─ result: !mogg.shape_func_result<4>
      │
      └─ mogg.output %s
         └─ return the shape value from this routine

The implementation creates one input pointer per input tensor, adds any input dynamic dimensions, and adds a context argument. It then reconstructs the input views and creates mogg.call.shape. There is no output tensor destination pointer for the shape result: the routine returns the shape by value. Source: routine construction and body

The context belongs to the routine boundary. The inner shape-function call receives its declared tensor operands; this gather helper’s signature takes input and indices, without a DeviceContext argument. Source: registered helper signature

Also, axis=-2 must survive this transformation:

output_rank=4 → how many dimension sizes to return
axis=-2      → which input axis gather replaces

Knowing rank alone would not tell the helper which axis to replace. The lowering forwards both output_rank and the original normalized kernel parameters. Source: parameter forwarding

5. How does the returned shape help subsequent computation?

Later, the MOGG→MGP lowering extracts each returned size and binds it to its corresponding dimension declaration. It also carries the completion dependency so subsequent work can use those dimensions. Source: extraction and binding

For our example, the relationship is:

Host shape routine executes
            │
            ▼
shapeResult = [1,4,5,3]
            │
            ├─ element 0 → D4 = 1
            ├─ element 1 → D5 = 4
            ├─ element 2 → D6 = 5
            └─ element 3 → D7 = 3
                            │
                            ▼
       Dependent tensor work can use [D4,D5,D6,D7]

The repository test uses those dimensions to broadcast scalar integer 1:

Shape calculation:
    returns [1,4,5,3]

Subsequent tensor calculation:
    broadcast scalar 1 to [1,4,5,3]

Illustrative tensor result:
    60 elements, each equal to 1

The test contains a shape-only gather invocation followed by broadcast; it does not perform a data gather. Its FileCheck assertions verify that axis and output_rank survive lowering. The numeric shape and 60 ones above explain the intended arithmetic; they are not captured execution results. Source: complete test

6. Example with dynamic input dimensions: the result type stays the same across executions.

Consider an illustrative gather invocation:

Input shape:   [N,8,64]
Indices shape: [L]
Axis:          1

Output shape:  [N,L,64]
Output rank:   3

Applying the same gather shape rule gives:

Execution A                    Execution B
───────────                    ───────────
N = 2                          N = 5
L = 3                          L = 7

Returned shape:                Returned shape:
[2,3,64]                       [5,7,64]

Return type in both:
!mogg.shape_func_result<3>

The sizes vary, but the number of returned sizes remains three. The lowering supplies dynamic input dimensions as routine arguments and uses them when reconstructing the input tensor views. Sources: dynamic dimensions and views, gather shape rule

Input pointers + runtime dimensions N,L
                    │
                    ▼
       Reconstructed input tensor views
                    │
                    ▼
              Host shape helper
                    │
                    ▼
        [current N, current L, 64]

7. Example where the helper must inspect actual tensor values.

Some output shapes depend on the data, even when the input shape is fixed.

The repository’s mo.arg_nonzero shape helper returns:

[number of nonzero elements, input rank]

It scans the input, counts nonzero values, and returns those two dimensions. Source: counting implementation

For an illustrative input:

X = [[0,7,0],
     [4,0,9]]

Input shape: [2,3]
Input rank:  2

Nonzero positions:
    [0,1]
    [1,0]
    [1,2]

Count: 3

The two calculations are separate:

                    X
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
    Shape helper        Subsequent data kernel
    counts nonzeros     produces coordinates
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
    returns [3,2]       [[0,1],
                         [1,0],
                         [1,2]]

    Shape-result type:
    !mogg.shape_func_result<2>

The shape helper returns [3,2]; the coordinates are the tensor data produced by the operation’s data kernel.

With a different input of the same shape:

X = [[0,0,0],
     [0,5,0]]

Returned shape: [1,2]
Same shape-result type: !mogg.shape_func_result<2>

Because this helper reads element values, it needs accessible input storage. For data-dependent operands residing on a GPU, the fallback machinery inserts a transfer to the host before the host shape calculation. That transfer obtains the current data during execution. Source: host transfer handling

For the fused-attention example, the caller explicitly supplies output shape [32,32]. Those dimensions are already known, so this particular host shape-function path is not needed to discover the attention output shape. Source: attention output type

#ifndef GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_CONVERSION_MAPTOMOGG_TD
#define GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_CONVERSION_MAPTOMOGG_TD

include "mlir/Pass/PassBase.td"

def MAPToMOGG : Pass<"map-to-mogg", "mlir::ModuleOp"> {
  let summary = "Lower `map` dialect kernels into `mogg` codegen ops.";
  let description = [{
    Lowers `map` dialect kernels into `mogg` codegen ops: dynamic dims become
    SSA values, contexts are added, and tensors are built from pointers. This is
    where the fusion-focused `map` IR crosses into the code-generation-focused
    `mogg` IR.
  }];

  let options = [
    Option<"enableComputeLambdas", "enable-compute-lambdas", "bool",
      /*default=*/"true",
      "Build compute lambdas for epilogues feeding a kernel argument that "
      "declares `_FusedComputeOutputTensor`. When false, such an epilogue gets "
      "a classic store lambda instead.">,
  ];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
    "M::MO::MODialect",
    "M::MOSH::MOSHDialect",
  ];
}

#endif // GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_CONVERSION_MAPTOMOGG_TD

#ifndef GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_INTERFACES_MAPTOMOGGSTATE_H
#define GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_INTERFACES_MAPTOMOGGSTATE_H

#include "GraphCompiler/MODialect/MODevices.h"
#include "GraphCompiler/MOGGDialect/Analysis/MojoRegistry.h"
#include "mlir/IR/Builders.h"
#include "mlir/IR/IRMapping.h"
#include "mlir/Support/LogicalResult.h"
#include "llvm/ADT/MapVector.h"
#include "llvm/ADT/STLFunctionalExtras.h"

namespace M::MO {
class InvokeShapeFuncOp;
} // namespace M::MO

namespace M::MAP {

// Per-kernel context for MAPToMOGG's recursive lowering of one
// `map.iter.opaque` (see `LowerableToMOGGInterface`); rebuilt per kernel.
struct MAPToMOGGState {
  MAPToMOGGState(MOGG::MojoRegistry &registry, mlir::Operation *op)
      : registry(registry), builder(op) {}

  MOGG::MojoRegistry &registry;
  mlir::OpBuilder builder;

  // Whether an epilogue feeding a `_FusedComputeOutputTensor` may become a
  // compute lambda; mirrors the `EmitMojo` option.
  bool enableComputeLambdas = true;

  // Maps the kernel's inputs and output block args (and epilogue results) to
  // their reconstructed `!mogg.tensor`s. Nested regions remap their own
  // entries before lowering their body.
  mlir::IRMapping mapping;

  // Set by `IterOpaqueOp::lowerToMOGG` before any nested op is lowered.
  DeviceRefAttr device;
  // Unique dynamic dims, in first-seen order, to their `!mogg.dim` block
  // args (null until the block args exist).
  llvm::MapVector<mlir::Attribute, mlir::BlockArgument> dimArgs;
  // The trailing `!mogg.context` block args: one, or one per device (in
  // `getUniqueDevicesFromKernel` order) for a distributed kernel taking a
  // `DeviceContextArray`, which `ConformCallOperands` packs into a tuple.
  llvm::SmallVector<mlir::Value> contextArgs;

  // Each dynamic index op in a functor body (a `map.index.reshape` or a
  // `map.index.slice.select`), to the `!mogg.shape` captures it evaluates
  // against at runtime.
  llvm::DenseMap<mlir::Operation *, llvm::SmallVector<mlir::Value>>
      indexShapeArgs;

  mlir::LogicalResult lowerOp(mlir::Operation *op);
  // Lowers `block`'s ops in order, skipping those `shouldLower` rejects; a
  // predicate may rely on earlier ops already being mapped.
  mlir::LogicalResult lowerRegionBody(
      mlir::Block &block,
      llvm::function_ref<bool(mlir::Operation *)> shouldLower =
          [](mlir::Operation *) { return true; });
};

/// Lowers a `mo.invoke_shape_func` into a `mogg.routine`, and erases it.
mlir::LogicalResult lowerInvokeShapeFuncToMOGG(MO::InvokeShapeFuncOp op,
                                               MAPToMOGGState &state);

} // namespace M::MAP

#endif // GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_INTERFACES_MAPTOMOGGSTATE_H

//
